title: Faint galaxies let JWST test dark matter in the early universe
topic: Cosmology & Early Universe / Gravity & Fundamental Physics
freshness: Unreviewed preprint submitted to arXiv on October 27, 2026; selected within the preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: JWST has counted galaxies so faint and distant that they can test how matter gathered on small scales about 750 million years after the Big Bang. A preliminary analysis finds that those galaxy counts are consistent with cold dark matter and sets an independent limit on one warm-dark-matter model.
whyItMatters: Dark matter does not shine, but its gravity built the halos in which early galaxies formed. Measuring faint galaxies at a young cosmic age gives researchers a new way to test dark-matter behavior before billions of years of mergers and stellar feedback complicated the evidence.

body:
## Tiny galaxies as dark matter detectors

Dark matter cannot be photographed, but JWST may have found a way to test how it clumped when the universe was only about 750 million years old. The clue comes from extremely faint galaxies whose existence depends on small dark matter halos forming first.

A new analysis uses observations from GLIMPSE, a JWST program aimed through the galaxy cluster Abell S1063. The cluster bends and magnifies light from much more distant objects, acting as a natural telescope. This gravitational lensing allowed GLIMPSE to measure galaxies down to an ultraviolet absolute magnitude of about -12, fainter than earlier surveys could reliably reach. The researchers combined those measurements with Hubble and Subaru data covering redshifts 4 to 8.

They studied the ultraviolet luminosity function, which is a census of how many star-forming galaxies exist at each brightness. The faint end matters because small galaxies are expected to live inside small dark matter halos. If dark matter struggled to gather on small scales, fewer of those halos and galaxies should exist.

## From galaxy counts to invisible structure

The team translated the galaxy census into a matter power spectrum. This quantity describes how strongly matter density varies across different physical scales. Their inferred spectrum agrees with the standard cold-dark-matter prediction down to sub-megaparsec scales. The reported uncertainty is 0.2 dex for wavenumbers of 3 to 9 per megaparsec and 0.5 dex from 9 to 27 per megaparsec. A dex is a logarithmic unit: 0.2 dex corresponds to a factor of about 1.6, while 0.5 dex is about a factor of 3.2.

Cold dark matter moves slowly enough in the early universe to preserve small density variations. Warm dark matter would erase some of them, reducing the supply of low-mass halos. For a specific model in which warm dark matter began as a thermal relic, the authors infer that its particle mass must exceed 3.2 kiloelectronvolts at 95 percent confidence. This is the strongest such limit yet from the reionization era, although lower-redshift studies already set tighter limits using other methods. Its value is independence: it tests a much earlier epoch with different assumptions and sources of error.

## What was seen, and what was inferred

**Measured:** JWST, Hubble, and Subaru counted ultraviolet-bright galaxies across a range of early cosmic times. GLIMPSE extended that census to unusually faint galaxies by using cluster lensing.

**Inferred:** The abundance of those galaxies is consistent with cold dark matter on the small scales tested, and it disfavors thermal warm-dark-matter particles lighter than 3.2 kiloelectronvolts under the authors' model. This is not a direct detection of a dark matter particle.

The translation is difficult because starlight does not map perfectly onto halo mass. Star formation can occur in bursts, dust can hide ultraviolet light, and lens models and cosmic variance affect the faintest counts. The abundance of early halos is also less firmly calibrated for nonstandard dark matter. The authors varied several galaxy-formation and halo-model parameters, tested alternate dust and lensing treatments, and removed the faintest bins; they report that the main constraints stayed similar.

The paper is an unreviewed preprint, so its result remains preliminary. Even so, it shows why JWST's faintest galaxies are useful beyond galaxy studies: each one is evidence that an unseen gravitational scaffold had already formed on a small scale in the young universe.
